column9: Which elements are in magnesium sulfate, MgSO₄?
column28: Mg is magnesium, S is sulfur, and O is oxygen. Manganese is Mn, not Mg, and sodium is Na, which is not in the formula. The O counts as its own element.
column29: Mg and Mn look alike. Check the second letter of each symbol on the periodic table.

column9: In the formula N₂O₅, which number tells you how many nitrogen atoms there are?
column28: The subscript 2 comes right after N, so there are 2 nitrogen atoms. The 5 belongs to O (5 oxygen atoms). 7 is the total, and 10 comes from multiplying, which is not how subscripts work.
column29: A subscript counts the symbol it comes right after.

column9: In H₂O, the small 2 written below and to the right of the H is called a –
column28: A subscript is the small number below and to the right of a symbol. It counts only the atoms of the symbol it follows. A coefficient is a big number in front of the whole formula.
column29: Sub- means below, like a submarine goes below the water.

column9: Which formula has exactly 2 atoms in one unit?
column28: HCl has 1 H + 1 Cl = 2 atoms. H₂O has 3, NH₃ has 4, and CO₂ has 3.
column29: Add the atoms in each formula. No subscript means 1.

column9: Oxygen check: which formula unit below contains more oxygen atoms than any of the others?
column28: K₂CO₃: 3. CuSO₄: 4. Mg(NO₃)₂: 3 × 2 = 6. Na₃PO₄: 4. Mg(NO₃)₂ has the most because the outside 2 doubles the oxygen inside the parentheses.
column29: Count O in each one. Don't forget the outside subscript on the parentheses.

column9: Nia says one formula unit of iron(III) hydroxide, Fe(OH)₃, has 1 hydrogen atom. What mistake did she make?
column14: She forgot that the outside 3 multiplies the H inside the parentheses
column15: She added the numbers instead of multiplying them
column16: She counted the iron atom as hydrogen
column17: She made no mistake; H has no subscript, so there is 1
column28: H starts at 1 inside the parentheses, but the outside 3 multiplies everything inside: H = 1 × 3 = 3 (and O = 3). Nia counted only what is written inside.
column29: Draw an arrow from the outside 3 to every atom inside the parentheses.

column9: Maya notices that H₂O and CO₂ both have 3 atoms per molecule. She says they must be the same substance. Is she right?
column14: Yes, because the same number of atoms makes the same substance
column15: Yes, because both formulas have a subscript of 2
column16: No, because they are made of different elements in different combinations
column17: No, because H₂O has more total atoms than CO₂
column28: A formula tells which elements and how many of each. H₂O is 2 H + 1 O; CO₂ is 1 C + 2 O. Different elements make different substances, even with the same total of 3 atoms.
column29: Look at which elements are in each formula, not just how many atoms.

column9: A compound has 2 aluminum atoms, 3 carbon atoms, and 9 oxygen atoms in one formula unit. Which formula matches?
column28: Al₂(CO₃)₃: Al 2, C 1 × 3 = 3, O 3 × 3 = 9. Al₂CO₃ has only 1 C and 3 O; Al₃(CO₃)₂ has 3 Al; Al(CO₃)₃ has 1 Al.
column29: Count Al, C, and O in each choice, using the outside subscript on everything inside the parentheses.

column9: Why do atoms form chemical bonds?
column17: To lose all of their electrons
column28: Atoms bond to be stable, usually by getting 8 electrons in their outer shell. Bonding does not change which element an atom is.
column29: Think about the octet rule. What do atoms get when their outer shell is full?

column9: Which property is typical of an ionic compound?
column14: Low melting point; often a liquid or gas
column15: High melting point and forms crystals
column16: Does not conduct electricity when dissolved
column28: Ionic compounds generally melt above 300 °C and form crystals. The other choices describe covalent compounds.
column29: Ionic bonds are strong. Does that make the compound easy or hard to melt?

column9: Which compound is made only of nonmetals, so it is covalent?
column28: Carbon and oxygen are both nonmetals, so CO is covalent. NaBr, MgS, and LiCl each start with a metal (Na, Mg, Li), so they are ionic.
column29: Look for the formula with no metal in it. Metals sit left of the staircase.

column9: Lithium and oxygen bond to make Li₂O. What type of compound is Li₂O?
column14: Ionic, because lithium is a metal and oxygen is a nonmetal
column15: Covalent, because lithium and oxygen are both nonmetals
column16: Covalent, because it has two lithium atoms
column17: Neither, because lithium and oxygen cannot bond
column28: Lithium (Group 1) is a metal and oxygen is a nonmetal, so Li₂O is ionic. The number of atoms does not decide the bond type.
column29: Is lithium left or right of the staircase? Is oxygen?

column9: Magnesium and oxygen bond to form a compound. What happens to the electrons?
column17: No electrons move; the atoms just stick
column28: Mg is a metal and O is a nonmetal, so the bond is ionic: the metal transfers electrons to the nonmetal. Sharing happens only between nonmetals.
column29: Is this metal + nonmetal or nonmetal + nonmetal? Then: which one gives electrons away?

column9: Maya dissolves an unknown white solid in water. The solution lights up the conductivity tester. What does this suggest about the solid?
column14: It is covalent, because only covalent compounds dissolve in water
column15: It is covalent, because it is a white solid
column16: It is ionic, because every compound that dissolves is ionic
column17: It is ionic, because it breaks into free-moving ions in water
column28: Ionic compounds conduct electricity when dissolved because they break into free-moving ions that carry the current. Dissolving by itself proves nothing (sugar dissolves too), and color is irrelevant.
column29: What has to be moving around in the water for electricity to flow?

column9: Jae dissolves sugar in water and tests it. The bulb does not light. Why doesn't the sugar solution conduct electricity?
column14: Sugar stays as whole molecules, so there are no ions to carry current
column15: Sugar is ionic, but its ions are too large to move
column16: Sugar does not actually dissolve in water
column17: The water blocks electricity from reaching the sugar
column28: Sugar is covalent. When it dissolves, it stays as whole molecules, so there are no charged ions to carry current. Ionic compounds like KI break into free-moving ions and do conduct.
column29: Is sugar made of metals and nonmetals, or only nonmetals? What does that mean for ions?

column9: Aluminum oxide is Al₂O₃. Which classification and reason are correct?
column14: Covalent, because aluminum is in Group 13, not Group 1 or 2
column15: Ionic, because aluminum is left of the staircase (a metal) and oxygen is a nonmetal
column16: Covalent, because it has more oxygen atoms than aluminum atoms
column17: Ionic, because oxygen is a metal
column28: Aluminum is a metal (left of the staircase) and oxygen is a nonmetal, so Al₂O₃ is ionic. The number of atoms does not decide bond type, and metals are not only in Groups 1 and 2.
column29: Find aluminum on the periodic table. Which side of the staircase is it on?

column9: A student says, "Water must be ionic, because salt dissolves in it." Water melts at 0 °C. Which is the best evaluation of the claim?
column14: Correct: anything that can dissolve salt must be ionic
column15: Correct: water and salt are found together in the ocean, so they are the same type
column16: Wrong: water is made of two nonmetals and melts far below 300 °C, so it is covalent; dissolving salt says nothing about water's bonds
column17: Wrong: water is a liquid, and liquids can never be ionic
column28: Water (H₂O) is hydrogen and oxygen, two nonmetals, and its 0 °C melting point is far below 300 °C, so it is covalent. What water can dissolve is irrelevant evidence. Saying liquids can never be ionic reaches the right answer for a wrong reason.
column29: Ignore the salt. What are water's own elements, and what does its melting point tell you?

column9: Acetate is C₂H₃O₂⁻, ammonium is NH₄⁺, and hydroxide is OH⁻. Which list contains ONLY ionic compounds?
column28: NaC₂H₃O₂ (metal + acetate), CuO (copper is a metal), and NH₄I (ammonium) are all ionic. Each other list hides one covalent compound: CH₄, N₂O, or CO₂.
column29: In each list, hunt for a compound with no metal and no polyatomic ion.
